# Numerical Solution of Differential-Algebraic Equations > Index Reduction for DAEs > Index Reduction of Partial Differential Algebraic Equations (PDAE):

Consider the following system of partial differential equations:

(∂u/∂t) + (∂v/∂t) = (∂^2u/∂x^2) + u(∂v/∂x) - v(∂u/∂x) + (2π t)^2v, 
	(∂^2v/∂x^2) + (2π t)^2u=0, 
	u(0, t)=v(0, t)=0, 
	u(1, t)=sin(2π t), Subscript[((∂v/∂x)), x = 1]=2 π t cos(2 π t), 
	u(x, 0)=v(x, 0)=0.

In the above system, the second PDE does not contain a time derivative component for any of the variables. Therefore, ``NDSolve`` cannot solve this system using method of lines because the resulting mass-matrix will be singular and the system has an index of 1. To reduce the index of the system, the above system is represented in a matrix-vector form as

(dU/dt) + (dV/dt)=A.U + U (B.V) - V (B.U) + (2 π t)^2V, 
	C.V + (2 π t)^2U=0.

The terms A, B, C represent the matrices obtained by discretizing the spatial derivatives and the terms U, V represent the vectors obtained by discretizing the variables u(x, t), v(x, t) at discrete spatial intervals Subscript[x, i]. Index reduction is performed on the new system using the index-reduction methods described above. The resulting index-reduced system is

(dU/dt) + (dV/dt)=A.U + U (B.V) - V (B.U) + (2 π t)^2V, 
	C.(dV/dt) + (2 π t)^2(dU/dt) + (8 π^2 t)U=0.

The spatial derivatives are now reintroduced back into the system to give

(∂u/∂t) + (∂v/∂t)=(∂^2u/∂x^2) + u(∂v/∂x) - v(∂u/∂x) + (2π t)^2v, 
	(∂^3v/∂x^2∂t) + (2π t)^2(∂u/∂t) + (8π t)^2u=0.

The resulting system can then be solved using traditional methods available in ``NDSolve``.

Define the system:

```wl
In[1]:=
eqns = {D[u[x, t], t] - D[v[x, t], t] == D[u[x, t], x, x] + u[x, t] D[v[x, t], x] - v[x, t] D[u[x, t], x] + (2 Pi t) ^ 2 v[x, t], D[v[x, t], x, x] + (2 Pi t) ^ 2 u[x, t] == 0};
bcs = {u[0, t] == v[0, t] == 0, u[1, t] == Sin[2 Pi t], Derivative[1, 0][v][1, t] == 2 Pi t Cos[2 Pi t]};
ics = {u[x, 0] == v[x, 0] == 0};
```

Solve the system by doing index reduction on the PDAE:

```wl
In[2]:= sol  = NDSolveValue[{eqns, bcs, ics}, {u, v}, {x, 0, 1}, {t, 0, 3}, Method -> {"IndexReduction" -> Automatic, "EquationSimplification" -> "Residual", "PDEDiscretization" -> {"MethodOfLines", "SpatialDiscretization" -> {"TensorProductGrid", "MinPoints" -> 200, "MaxPoints" -> 200}}}]

Out[2]= {InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 1.}, {0., 3.}}, <>], InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 1.}, {0., 3.}}, <>]}
```

Note that 200 points were used for the spatial discretization because the default spatial grid spacing based on the constant initial condition is insufficient to handle the variation the solution develops over time.

Plot the solution:

```wl
In[3]:= Plot3D[Evaluate[#[x, t]], {x, 0, 1}, {t, 0, 3}]& /@ sol

Out[3]= <image removed>
```

It is important to note that the index reduction is performed in the time derivative, so no new boundary conditions are needed or added to the system. However, if the PDAE is found to be of high index, then additional initial conditions may be needed.

</result>

# "EventLocator" Method for NDSolve > Examples > Poincaré Sections > The Hénon–Heiles System

Define the Hénon–Heiles system that models stellar motion in a galaxy.

This gets the Hénon–Heiles system from the ``NDSolveProblems`` package:

```wl
In[1]:=
system = GetNDSolveProblem["HenonHeiles"];
vars = system["DependentVariables"];eqns = {system["System"], system["InitialConditions"]}

Out[1]= {{Derivative[1][Subscript[Y, 1]][T] == Subscript[Y, 3][T], Derivative[1][Subscript[Y, 2]][T] == Subscript[Y, 4][T], Derivative[1][Subscript[Y, 3]][T] == -Subscript[Y, 1][T] (1 + 2 Subscript[Y, 2][T]), Derivative[1][Subscript[Y, 4]][T] == -Subscript[Y, 1][T]^2 + (-1 + Subscript[Y, 2][T]) Subscript[Y, 2][T]}, {Subscript[Y, 1][0] == (3/25), Subscript[Y, 2][0] == (3/25), Subscript[Y, 3][0] == (3/25), Subscript[Y, 4][0] == (3/25)}}
```

The Poincaré section of interest in this case is the collection of points in the Subscript[Y, 2] - Subscript[Y, 4] plane when the orbit passes through Subscript[Y, 1]=0.

Since the actual result of the numerical integration is not required, it is possible to avoid storing all the data in ``InterpolatingFunction`` by specifying the output variables list (in the second argument to ``NDSolve``) as empty, or ``{}``. This means that ``NDSolve`` will produce no ``InterpolatingFunction`` as output, avoiding storing a lot of unnecessary data. ``NDSolve`` does give a message ``NDSolve::noout`` warning there will be no output functions, but it can safely be turned off in this case since the data of interest is collected from the event actions.

The linear interpolation event location method is used because the purpose of the computation here is to view the results in a graph with relatively low resolution. If you were doing an example where you needed to zoom in on the graph to great detail or to find a feature, such as a fixed point of the Poincaré map, it would be more appropriate to use the default location method.

This turns off the message warning about no output:

```wl
In[2]:= Off[NDSolve::noout];
```

This integrates the Hénon–Heiles system using a fourth-order explicit Runge–Kutta method with fixed step size of 0.25. The event action is to use ``Sow`` on the values of Subscript[Y, 2] and Subscript[Y, 4] :

```wl
In[3]:=
data = 
	Reap[
	NDSolve[eqns, {}, {T, 10000}, 
	Method -> {"EventLocator", "Event" -> Subscript[Y, 1][T], "EventAction" :> Sow[{Subscript[Y, 2][T], Subscript[Y, 4][T]}], "EventLocationMethod" -> "LinearInterpolation", 
	"Method" -> {"FixedStep", "Method" -> {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "DifferenceOrder" -> 4}}}, 
	StartingStepSize -> 0.25, MaxSteps -> ∞];
	];
```

This plots the Poincaré section. The collected data is found in the last part of the result of ``Reap`` and the list of points is the first part of that:

```wl
In[4]:=
psdata = data[[-1, 1]];
ListPlot[psdata, Axes -> False, Frame -> True, AspectRatio -> 1]

Out[4]= <image removed>
```

Since the Hénon–Heiles system is Hamiltonian, a symplectic method gives much better qualitative results for this example.

This integrates the Hénon–Heiles system using a fourth-order symplectic partitioned Runge–Kutta method with fixed step size of 0.25. The event action is to use ``Sow`` on the values of Subscript[Y, 2] and Subscript[Y, 4] :

```wl
In[5]:=
sdata = 
	Reap[
	NDSolve[eqns, {}, {T, 10000}, 
	Method -> {"EventLocator", "Event" -> Subscript[Y, 1][T], "EventAction" :> Sow[{Subscript[Y, 2][T], Subscript[Y, 4][T]}], "EventLocationMethod" -> "LinearInterpolation", 
	"Method" -> {"SymplecticPartitionedRungeKutta", "DifferenceOrder" -> 4, "PositionVariables" -> {Subscript[Y, 1][T], Subscript[Y, 2][T]}}}, 
	StartingStepSize -> 0.25, MaxSteps -> ∞];
	];
```

This plots the Poincaré section. The collected data is found in the last part of the result of ``Reap`` and the list of points is the first part of that:

```wl
In[6]:=
psdata = sdata[[-1, 1]];
ListPlot[psdata, Axes -> False, Frame -> True, AspectRatio -> 1]

Out[6]= <image removed>
```

</result>

# Numerical Solution of Differential-Algebraic Equations > Index Reduction for DAEs

The built-in solvers for DAEs in ``NDSolve`` currently handle index-1 systems of DAEs fully automatically. For higher-index systems, an index reduction is necessary to get to a solution. This index reduction can be performed by giving appropriate options to ``NDSolve``.

``NDSolve`` uses symbolic techniques to do index reduction. This means that if your DAE system is expressed in the form F(t, x, Derivative[1][x])=0, where ``NDSolve`` cannot see how the components of x interact and compute symbolic derivatives, the index reduction cannot be done, and for this reason ``NDSolve`` does not do index reduction, by default.

For an example, consider the classic DAE describing the motion of a pendulum:

m Derivative[2][x](t) + λ(t)x(t) = 0, 
	m Derivative[2][y](t) + λ(t) y(t) = -g, 
	x^2(t) + y^2(t) = L,

where there is a mass m at the point {x(t), y(t)} constrained by a string of length L. λ is a Lagrange multiplier that is effectively the tension in the string. For simplicity in the description of index reduction, take m=L=g=1. The figure shows the schematic of the pendulum system.

<image removed>

Sketch of the forces acting on a pendulum.

If the index of the system is not obvious from the equations, one thing to do is try it in ``NDSolve``, and if the solver is not able to solve it, in many cases it is able to generate a message indicating what the index appears to be for the initial conditions specified.

Define equations and a complete set of initial values for the constrained pendulum system:

```wl
In[1]:=
cpdae = {x''[t] + λ[t] x[t] == 0, y''[t] + λ[t] y[t] == -1, x[t] ^ 2 + y[t] ^ 2 == 1};
cpinit = {x[0] == 1, x'[0] == 0, x''[0] == 0, y[0] == 0, y'[0] == 0, y''[0] == -1, λ[0] == 0};
```

Try to solve the constrained pendulum system:

```wl
In[2]:= NDSolve[{cpdae, cpinit}, {x, y, λ}, {t, 0, 100}]

NDSolve::index: The DAE solver failed at ⁠t⁠ = ⁠0.000339613⁠. The solver is intended for index 1 DAE systems and structural analysis indicates that the DAE index is ⁠3⁠. The option Method->{"IndexReduction"->Automatic} may be used to reduce the index of the system.

Out[2]= <image removed>
```

The message indicates that the index is 3, indicating that index reduction is necessary to solve the system. Note that a complete consistent initialization is used here to avoid possible issues with initialization. This aspect of the solution procedure is treated in ["Consistent Initialization of DAEs"](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDAE#1465474060)with more detail.

The option setting ``Method -> {"IndexReduction" -> {irmeth, iropts}}`` is used to specify that ``NDSolve`` uses index reduction method ``irmeth`` with general index reduction options ``iropts``.

|                    |                                   |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| None               | no index reduction (default)      |
| Automatic          | choose the method automatically   |
| "Pantelides"       | graph-based Pantelides algorithm  |
| "StructuralMatrix" | structural matrix-based algorithm |

Index reduction methods.

The following options can be given for all index reduction methods.

|                    |           |                                                 |
| ------------------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| "ConstraintMethod" | Automatic | how to handle constraints from specified system |
| "IndexGoal"        | Automatic | index to reduce to (1 or 0)                     |

Options for index reduction.

Solve using automatically chosen methods of index reduction:

```wl
In[3]:= sol = First[NDSolve[{cpdae, cpinit}, {x, y, λ}, {t, 0, 100}, Method -> {"IndexReduction" -> Automatic}, MaxSteps -> ∞]]

Out[3]= <image removed>

In[4]:= Plot[Evaluate[{x[t], y[t]} /. %], {t, 0, 100}]

Out[4]= <image removed>
```

Index reduction is done by differentiating equations in the DAE system. Suppose that an equation ``eqn`` is differentiated during the process of index reduction so that ``deqn = (d/dt)eqn`` is included in the system in place of ``eqn``. Once the differentiation has been done, the differentiated equations comprise a fully determined system and can be solved on their own. However, it is typically important to incorporate the original equations in the system as constraints. How this is done is controlled by the ``"ConstraintMethod"`` index reduction option.

|     |     |
| --- | --- |
| None | do not keep the original equations as constraints and just solve with the differentiation equations |
| "DummyDerivatives" | use the method of Mattson and Soderlind [MS93] to replace some derivatives with algebraic variables (dummy derivatives) |
| "Projection" | reduce the index to 0 to get an ODE and use the "Projection" time integration method with the original equations that were differentiated as invariants |

Constraint methods.

Use index reduction and solve with the differentiated equations:

```wl
In[5]:= ucsol = First[NDSolve[{cpdae, cpinit}, {x, y, λ}, {t, 0, 100}, Method -> {"IndexReduction" -> {Automatic, "ConstraintMethod" -> None}}, MaxSteps -> ∞]];
```

Compare how well the constraint x^2 + y^2=1 is satisfied for the two solutions:

```wl
In[6]:= LogPlot[Evaluate[Abs[x[t] ^ 2 + y[t] ^ 2 - 1] /. {sol, ucsol}], {t, 0, 100}]

Out[6]= <image removed>
```

In the numerical solution with just the differentiated equations, the length of the pendulum is drifting away from 1. Incorporating the original equations into the solution as constraints is an important aspect of index reduction.

The next two sections will describe index reduction algorithms, followed by an explanation of constraint methods that can be used in ``NDSolve``.

</result>

# Numerical Solution of Differential-Algebraic Equations > Index Reduction for DAEs > Index Reduction Algorithms > Pantelides Method

The method proposed by Pantelides [[P88](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#1588312117)] is a graph theoretical method that was originally proposed for finding consistent initialization of DAEs. It works with a bipartite graph of dependent variables and equations, and when the algorithm can find a traversal of the graph, then the system has been reduced to index at most 1. A traversal in this sense effectively means an ordering of variables and equations so that the graph's incidence matrix has no zeros on the diagonal.

When the bipartite graph does not have a complete traversal, the algorithm effectively augments the path by differentiating equations, introducing new variables (derivatives of previous variables) in the process. Unless the original system is structurally singular, the algorithm will terminate with a traversal. Generally, the algorithm does only the differentiations needed to get the traversal, but since it is a greedy algorithm, it is not always the minimal number.

It is beyond the scope of this documentation to describe the algorithm in detail. The implementation built into the Wolfram Language follows the algorithm outlined in [[P88](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#1588312117)] fairly closely. It uses ``Graph`` to efficiently implement the graph computations and symbolically differentiates the equations with ``D`` when differentiation is called for.

When there is a traversal of the system, it is then possible to find an ordering for the variables and equations such that the incidence matrix is in block lower triangular (BLT) form. The BLT form is used in setting up the dummy derivative method for maintaining constraints and also in the ``"StateSpace"`` time integration method. A description of the [BLT ordering](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveStateSpace#1816117483) is included in ["State Space Method for DAEs"](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveStateSpace).

To begin index reduction on the constrained pendulum system ([2),](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDAE#1585047709) consider the variables {x'', y'', λ}. Generally, start with the highest-order derivative that appears in the equations. As a reminder, the pendulum equations are

m Derivative[2][x](t) + λ(t) x(t)=0, 
	m Derivative[2][y](t) + λ(t) y(t)=-g, 
	x^2(t) + y^2(t) = L^2

and the graph incidence matrix with respect to the highest-order derivative is

(⁠|   |   |   |
| - | - | - |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |⁠).

The incidence matrix is constructed by checking the presence of a variable in an equation. If the variable exists in the equation, a weight of 1 is given; if not then 0 is specified. So checking for the variables {Derivative[2][x], Derivative[2][y], λ} in the first equation gives {1, 0, 1} (as seen in the first row of the incidence matrix).

From the first incidence matrix, it is found that there is no traversal. The last equation is differentiated twice

Derivative[2][x] + λ x=0, 
	Derivative[2][y] + λ y=-1, 
	2x Derivative[2][x] + 2(Derivative[1][x])^2 + 2y Derivative[2][y] + 2(Derivative[1][y])^2=0.

The incidence matrix is now

(⁠|   |   |   |
| - | - | - |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 0 |⁠).

This can be reordered so that there is no zero on the diagonal by swapping the first and last equations, resulting in the incidence matrix

(⁠|   |   |   |
| - | - | - |
| 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |⁠).

The resulting system has index 1 since λ still appears as an algebraic variable and does not contain a derivative in the differentiated system. Differentiating the system one more time will provide a differential system for λ. Therefore, the index of the original system is indeed 3.

As a first approach, the system with the twice-differentiated equation can be solved directly.

Solve the system with the twice-differentiated equation:

```wl
In[1]:= d2sol = NDSolve[{x''[t] + λ[t] x[t] == 0, y''[t] + λ[t] y[t] == -1, D[x[t] ^ 2 + y[t] ^ 2 == 1, {t, 2}], cpinit}, {x, y, λ}, {t, 0, 100}, MaxSteps -> ∞]

NDSolve::pdord: Some of the functions have zero differential order, so the equations will be solved as a system of differential-algebraic equations.

Out[1]= <image removed>
```

Plot quantities that should be invariant, based on the originally specified equations:

```wl
In[2]:= Row[Table[Plot[Evaluate[D[x[t] ^ 2 + y[t] ^ 2 - 1, {t, i}] /. d2sol], {t, 0, 100}, ImageSize -> Small], {i, 0, 1}]]

Out[2]= <image removed><image removed>
```

The original pendulum length constraint is not being satisfied well; in fact, it stretches! The constraints are not satisfied well because the new system does not identically represent the original system. This can be seen by the fact that the new system does not contain the original constraint of x(t)^2 + y(t)^2=1, but rather its differentiated equations.

To model the original dynamics of the system with the new system, additional equations must be satisfied. However, including additional equations leads to more equations than unknowns. To address this issue, the method of dummy derivatives is used, so that the index-reduced system becomes balanced.

The Pantelides algorithm is efficient because it can use graph algorithms with well-controlled complexity even for very large problems. However, since it is based solely on incidence, there can be issues with systems that lead to Jacobians that are singular. The structural matrix method may be able to resolve such cases, but may have larger computational complexity for large systems.

</result>

# HeunG

HeunG[a, q, α, β, γ, δ, z] gives the general Heun function.

## Details

* ``HeunG`` belongs to the Heun class of functions, directly generalizes the ``Hypergeometric2F1`` function and occurs in quantum mechanics, mathematical physics and applications.

* Mathematical function, suitable for both symbolic and numerical manipulation.

* ``HeunG[a, q, α, β, γ, δ, z]`` satisfies the general Heun differential equation z (z - 1) (z - a) Derivative[2][y] + ((z - 1)(z - a)γ + z (z - a)δ + z (z - 1)(1 + α + β - γ - δ))y' + (α β z - q)y=0.

* The ``HeunG`` function is the regular solution of the general Heun equation that satisfies the condition ``HeunG[a, q, α, β, γ, δ, 0]=1``.

* ``HeunG`` has one branch cut discontinuity in the complex z plane running from 1 to ∞ and one running from a to ``DirectedInfinity[a]``.

* For certain special arguments, ``HeunG`` automatically evaluates to exact values.

* ``HeunG`` can be evaluated for arbitrary complex parameters.

* ``HeunG`` can be evaluated to arbitrary numerical precision.

* ``HeunG`` automatically threads over lists.

* ``HeunG[a, q, α, β, γ, δ, z]`` specializes to ``Hypergeometric2F1[α, β, γ, z]`` if q=a α β and δ=α + β - γ + 1 or a=1 and q=α β.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/HeunD#982511436'>

# HeunD

HeunD[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, z] gives the double-confluent Heun function.

## Details

* ``HeunD`` belongs to the Heun class of functions and occurs in quantum mechanics, mathematical physics and applications.

* Mathematical function, suitable for both symbolic and numerical manipulation.

* ``HeunD[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, z]`` satisfies the double-confluent Heun differential equation z^2Derivative[2][y] + (γ + δ z + ϵ z^2)Derivative[1][y] + (α z - q)y=0.

* The ``HeunD`` function is the power-series solution y(z) of the double-confluent Heun equation that satisfies the conditions y(1)=1 and Derivative[1][y](1)=0.

* For certain special arguments, ``HeunD`` automatically evaluates to exact values.

* ``HeunD`` can be evaluated for arbitrary complex parameters.

* ``HeunD`` can be evaluated to arbitrary numerical precision.

* ``HeunD`` automatically threads over lists.

### Basic Examples

Evaluate numerically:

```wl
In[1]:= HeunD[4, -0.6, -0.7 , -0.18, 0.3 , 0.12]

Out[1]= 6.94565
```

# HeunC

HeunC[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, z] gives the confluent Heun function.

## Details

* ``HeunC`` belongs to the Heun class of functions and occurs in quantum mechanics, mathematical physics and applications.

* Mathematical function, suitable for both symbolic and numerical manipulation.

* ``HeunC[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, z]`` satisfies the confluent Heun differential equation z(z - 1) Derivative[2][y] + (γ (z - 1) + δ z + z(z - 1) ϵ) y' + (α z - q)y=0.

* The ``HeunC`` function is the regular solution of the confluent Heun equation that satisfies the condition ``HeunC[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, 0]=1``.

* ``HeunC`` has a branch cut discontinuity in the complex z plane running from 1 to ∞.

* For certain special arguments, ``HeunC`` automatically evaluates to exact values.

* ``HeunC`` can be evaluated for arbitrary complex parameters.

* ``HeunC`` can be evaluated to arbitrary numerical precision.

* ``HeunC`` automatically threads over lists.

</result>

* The ``HeunB`` function is the regular solution of the bi-confluent Heun equation that satisfies the condition ``HeunB[q, α, γ, δ, ϵ, 0]=1``.

* For certain special arguments, ``HeunB`` automatically evaluates to exact values.

* ``HeunB`` can be evaluated for arbitrary complex parameters.

# DifferentialRoot

DifferentialRoot[lde][x] gives the holonomic function h(x), specified by the linear differential equation lde[h, x].

DifferentialRoot[lde] represents a pure holonomic function h.

## Details

* Mathematical function, suitable for both symbolic and numerical manipulation; also known as holonomic function and D-finite function.

* The holonomic function h(x) defined by a ``DifferentialRoot`` function satisfies a holonomic differential equation Subscript[p, n](x)Derivative[n][h](x) + Subscript[p, n - 1](x)h^(n - 1)(x)  + ⋯ + Subscript[p, 0](x)h(x) =0 with polynomial coefficients Subscript[p, i](x) and initial values h^(n - 1)(0)=Subscript[h, n - 1], ⋯, Derivative[1][h](0)=Subscript[h, 1], h(0)=Subscript[h, 0].

* ``DifferentialRoot`` can be used like any other mathematical function.

* ``FunctionExpand`` will attempt to convert ``DifferentialRoot`` functions in terms of special functions.

* The functions representable by ``DifferentialRoot`` include a large number of special functions.

* ``DifferentialRootReduce`` can convert most special functions to ``DifferentialRoot`` functions.

* Holonomic functions are closed under many operations, including:

|                                       |                                                                |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a h1(x), a h1(x) x^m                  | constant multiple, integer power                               |
| h1( x) + h2( x), h1(x) h2(x)          | sums and products                                              |
| h1(p(x)), h1(p1(x) / p2(x)), h1(a(x)) | composition with polynomial, rational, and algebraic functions |
| (h1⋆h2)(x)                           | convolution                                                    |
| (∂h1(x)/∂x), ∫h1(x)dx                 | derivatives and integrals                                      |

* ``DifferentialRoot`` is automatically generated by functions such as ``Integrate``, ``DSolve``, and ``GeneratingFunction``.

* Functions such as ``Integrate``, ``D``, ``SeriesCoefficient``, and ``DSolve`` work with ``DifferentialRoot`` inputs.

* ``DifferentialRoot`` can be evaluated to arbitrary numerical precision.

* ``DifferentialRoot`` automatically threads over lists.

* ``DifferentialRoot[lde, pred]`` represents a solution restricted to avoid cuts in the complex z plane defined by ``pred[z]``, where ``pred[z]`` can contain equations and inequalities.

# WFR > DVectorField > Examples > Applications > Hopf bifurcation analysis and first Lyapunov coefficient > 2

Compute the first Lyapunov coefficient for the following [predator-prey system](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Predator-prey_system) :

```wl
In[1]:=
Clear[X, μ]
PredatorPrey[{x_, y_}][{c_, d_, r_, α_}] := {r x(1 - x) - (c x y/x + α), -d y + (c x y/x + α)}
X = {x, y};
μ = {c, d, r, α};
Column[PredatorPrey[X][μ]]

Out[1]=
r (1 - x) x - (c x y/x + α)
-d y + (c x y/x + α)
```

The orbitally equivalent polynomial system:

```wl
In[2]:=
PolynomialPredatorPrey[{x_, y_}][{c_, d_, r_, α_}] := Evaluate@Map[Composition[Total, Factor, MonomialList[#, {x, y}]&, Expand, Factor, Times[#, x + α]&], PredatorPrey[X][μ]]
Column@PolynomialPredatorPrey[X][μ]

Out[2]=
-r x^3 - c x y - r x^2 (-1 + α) + r x α
(c - d) x y - d y α
```

The ``Jacobian`` matrix for the orbitally equivalent polynomial system:

```wl
In[3]:=
Clear[J]
J[{x_, y_}][{c_, d_, r_, α_}] := Evaluate[Simplify@D[PolynomialPredatorPrey[X][μ], {X}]]
MatrixForm@J[X][μ]

Out[82]//MatrixForm=
(⁠|                                      |                 |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------- |
| -c y + r (-3 x^2 - 2 x (-1 + α) + α) | -c x            |
| (c - d) y                            | c x - d (x + α) |⁠)
```

The non-trivial equilibrium point:

```wl
In[4]:=
Clear[X0]
X0[{c_, d_, r_, α_}] := Evaluate[Simplify[Normal[SolveValues[PolynomialPredatorPrey[X][μ] == 0 && Reduce[Thread[Flatten[{X, μ}] > 0]], X][[1]]]]]
MatrixForm@List@X0[μ]

Out[85]//MatrixForm= (⁠(d α/c - d)	(r α (c - d (1 + α))/(c - d)^2)⁠)
```

The linear approximation at $$X_{0}(\mu)$$ :

```wl
In[5]:=
Clear[J0]
J0[{c_, d_, r_, α_}] := Simplify@J[X0[μ]][μ]
MatrixForm@J0[μ]

Out[88]//MatrixForm=
(⁠|                                             |                |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| -(d r α (c (-1 + α) + d (1 + α))/(c - d)^2) | -(c d α/c - d) |
| (r α (c - d (1 + α))/c - d)                 | 0              |⁠)
```

Analyse the local stability with the resource function [BialternateSum](https://resources.wolframcloud.com/FunctionRepository/resources/BialternateSum/), with $$$\alpha$$$ as control parameter:

```wl
In[6]:= Reduce[Det[ResourceFunction["BialternateSum"][J0[μ]]] < 0 && 0 < d < c && r > 0 && α > 0, α]

Out[6]= d > 0 && c > d && r > 0 && α > (c - d/c + d)
```

The critical value of the Hopf bifurcation:

```wl
In[7]:= α0 = Part[Normal[SolveValues[Det[ResourceFunction["BialternateSum"][J0[μ]]] == 0 && 0 < d < c && r > 0 && α > 0, α]], 1]

Out[7]= (c - d/c + d)
```

Then, $$X_{0}(\mu)$$ is locally asymptotically stable for $$$\alpha>\alpha_{0}$$$ and locally asymptotically unstable for $$$\alpha<\alpha_{0}$$$ (with $$$c>d$$$), and can be confirmed by the transversality condition:

```wl
In[8]:= Factor[ReplaceAll[α -> α0][(1/2)D[Det[ResourceFunction["BialternateSum"][J0[μ]]], α]]]

Out[8]= -(d r/2 (c - d))
```

The non-trivial equilibrium point at $$$\alpha=\alpha_{0}$$$ :

```wl
In[9]:=
X0α0 = Simplify[X0[{c, d, r, α0}]];
MatrixForm@List@X0α0

Out[93]//MatrixForm= (⁠(d/c + d)	(c r/(c + d)^2)⁠)
```

Shift the non-trivial equilibrium point to the origin:

```wl
In[10]:=
PolynomialPredatorPrey[{ξ_, η_}][{c_, d_, r_}] := Evaluate@Map[Composition[Total, Collect[#, {ξ, η}, FullSimplify]&, MonomialList[#, {ξ, η}]&], ReplaceAll[Thread[{x, y} -> {ξ, η}]][PolynomialPredatorPrey[X + X0α0][{c, d, r, α0}]]]
X = {ξ, η};
μ3 = {c, d, r};
Column[PolynomialPredatorPrey[X][μ3]]

Out[10]=
-(c d η/c + d) - c η ξ - (d r ξ^2/c + d) - r ξ^3
(c (c - d) r ξ/(c + d)^2) + (c - d) η ξ
```

Verify that indeed the non-trivial equilibrium was shifted to the origin:

```wl
In[11]:= MatrixForm[{Simplify[ReplaceAll[{ξ -> -Part[X0α0, 1], η -> -Part[X0α0, 2]}][PolynomialPredatorPrey[X][μ3]]]}]

Out[98]//MatrixForm= (⁠0	0⁠)
```

The ``Jacobian`` matrix in the new state variables:

```wl
In[12]:=

Out[100]//MatrixForm=

| ----------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| -c η - (2 d r ξ/c + d) - 3 r ξ^2    | -(c d/c + d) - c ξ |
| (c (c - d) r/(c + d)^2) + (c - d) η | (c - d) ξ          |⁠)
```

Using both the linear approximation and its transpose at the origin, with $$$\alpha=\frac{c-d}{c+d}$$$ and $$$r=\frac{(c+d)^{3}\omega^{2}}{c^2(c-d)d}$$$, we obtain the eigenvalues $$$-i\omega$$$ and $$$i\omega$$$ :

```wl
In[16]:= Column[MatrixForm @* List /@ Eigenvalues /@ {J0[μ2], J0T[μ2]}, Spacings -> 1]
```

The critical eigenvectors $$$q$$$, $$$\overline{q}$$$, $$$p$$$, $$$\overline{p}$$$ :

```wl
q = -I ω(c + d) * Eigenvectors[J0[μ2]][[2]];
```

where

$$C_{1}=\langle p,C(q,q,\overline{q})+B(\overline{q},h_{20})+2B(q,h_{11}) \rangle$$

and $$$h_{20}$$$, $$$h_{11}$$$ are given by

$$$h_{20}=\left( 2i\omega I_{2\times2}-A \right)^{-1}B(q,q)$$$, $$$h_{11}=-A^{-1}B(q,q)$$$

```wl

h11 = Simplify[-Inverse[J0[μ2]].BB[q, qc][μ3]];
MatrixForm@List@h11

Out[140]//MatrixForm= (⁠0	-2 c d^2 r⁠)

In[28]:=
Clear[C1]
C1 = Simplify[ComplexExpand[pn.(CC[q, q, qc][μ3] + BB[qc, h20][μ3] + 2BB[q, h11][μ3])]]

Out[28]= -(1/3 (c + d)^2 ω)I c^2 (4 c^3 d ω^2 + 4 c d^3 ω (-3 I r + ω) + c^4 (d^2 + ω^2) + d^4 (d^2 - 5 d r + 4 r^2 - 6 I r ω + ω^2) + c^2 d^2 (-2 d^2 + 5 d r + 6 ω (-I r + ω)))
```

Finally, we compute the first Lyapunov coefficient:

```wl
In[29]:=

L1 = FullSimplify[(1/2ω)ComplexExpand[Re[C1]]]

Out[29]= -(c^2 d^2 r/ω)
```

Clearly, the first Lyapunov coefficient is strictly negative for all combinations of the fixed parameters. Therefore, a unique limit cycle emerges from the non-trivial equilibrium via Hopf bifurcation for $$$\alpha<\alpha_{0}$$$.

# WFR > DihedralODE > Description

Find the ordinary differential equation constraining periods of certain symmetrical curves

### Usage

``ResourceFunction["DihedralODE"][H, {λ, ϕ, α}]``
	returns the ODE constraining integral periods ``T``(``α``), given a Hamiltonian ``H`` such that ``α = H(λ, cos(k ϕ))``.

``ResourceFunction["DihedralODE"][H, {λ, ϕ, α}, rules]``
	first applies coordinate rewrite ``rules`` to ``H.``

``ResourceFunction["DihedralODE"][H, "Certificate"]``
	assumes default coordinate handling and returns a checked and checkable [Association](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/Association) containing proof data.
